title: Current electricity: from drift to power
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 12
OpenStax: Model of conduction in metals

chapters.title: Current and drift: charge in motion
chapters.formula: I = dQ/dt; I = neA v_d; conventional current is opposite electron drift
points: Current measures charge crossing a section per unit time.
Electrons move randomly plus slowly drift in a conductor.
The current direction is defined as positive-charge motion.
chapters.script: Welcome back. Today we begin current electricity by asking a very simple question: what does it mean for charge to flow? Current is the rate at which charge crosses a chosen cross section. For a steady flow, current is charge divided by time. More generally, I equals dQ by dt. Imagine a wire cut by an invisible ring. Every coulomb crossing that ring each second contributes one ampere. In a metal, electrons already move rapidly in random directions, but those random motions cancel on average. An electric field adds a tiny organized drift. That drift is slow, yet the electrical response of a circuit is established through the field throughout the conductor. Here is the microscopic connection. If n is the number of free electrons per unit volume, each with charge magnitude e, the cross-sectional area is A, and the drift speed is v sub d, then I equals n e A v sub d. Notice the product: in one second, a slice of length v sub d moves through area A. Its volume is A v sub d, so the number of carriers is n A v sub d. Each contributes charge e. One careful sign point: conventional current is defined in the direction positive charge would move. Electrons drift opposite to that direction. Try this: if two times ten to the 18 electrons cross a section each second, the current magnitude is three point two tenths of an ampere, using e equal to one point six times ten to the minus 19 coulomb. That direction convention will matter in every graph and circuit we meet next.

chapters.title: Drift speed, mobility and current density
chapters.formula: J = I/A = ne v_d; v_d = mu E; J = sigma E; sigma = ne mu
points: Current density removes the area factor and describes local flow.
Mobility connects drift speed to applied electric field in a simple conductor.
Conductivity and resistivity are reciprocal material properties.
chapters.script: The total current depends on how much wire we capture, so physicists also use current density. Current density J is current per cross-sectional area. For a uniform wire, J equals I over A, and the microscopic expression becomes n e v sub d. This is useful because it separates the local material response from the size of the wire. In a simple conductor, drift speed is proportional to the electric field: v sub d equals mobility times E. Mobility, written mu, tells us how easily carriers respond to the field. Combine those statements and J equals n e mu E. The factor n e mu is called conductivity, sigma, so J equals sigma E. Its reciprocal is resistivity, rho. Let us use a quick application. A wire carries two amperes through an area of one square millimeter. Convert the area to one times ten to the minus six square meters. The current density is therefore two times ten to the six amperes per square meter. It is not two amperes per millimeter in a vague sense; unit conversion is part of the physics. Now imagine the same current in a thinner wire. The current may be unchanged in a series path, but J becomes larger because A is smaller. That larger current density is associated with stronger heating risk. For JEE, keep the chain visible: microscopic carriers give drift speed, drift speed gives current density, and conductivity links current density to electric field. The equations are connected, not a collection of unrelated formulas.

chapters.title: Ohm's law and the I-V graph
chapters.formula: V = IR for an ohmic element; slope of V-versus-I graph is R
points: Ohm's law is a model relationship, not a universal rule for every device.
An ohmic resistor has a straight-line V-I relationship at fixed physical conditions.
Always inspect which quantity is on each graph axis before reading slope.
chapters.script: Now connect the field picture to a measurable circuit relation. For an ohmic conductor at fixed temperature and fixed physical conditions, potential difference is proportional to current. We write V equals I R. Resistance measures how strongly the element opposes charge flow in that condition. The phrase fixed conditions matters. A metal filament heats as current rises, so its resistance changes; a diode is even more clearly non-ohmic. On a graph, read the axes before grabbing a slope. If vertical is V and horizontal is I, the slope is R. If vertical is I and horizontal is V, the slope is one over R. That small habit prevents many JEE mistakes. Here is a short example. A resistor has twelve volts across it and carries three amperes. Its resistance is four ohms. If the same resistor remains at the same temperature and we apply twenty volts, the current becomes five amperes. Pause and ask: what assumption allowed that prediction? It was not merely the label resistor; it was the ohmic, fixed-condition model. The microscopic story also makes sense. A stronger field gives carriers more drift between collisions, so current density rises proportionally while the material and geometry stay stable. A graph that bends tells us the proportionality has changed. In practice, contact resistance, heating and material behavior can matter. In JEE questions, identify the model first, then use the graph or equation. Never call every two-terminal device ohmic just because it has a voltage and a current.

chapters.title: Resistance, resistivity and temperature
chapters.formula: R = rho L/A; rho(T) = rho0[1 + alpha(T - T0)] for a small temperature range
points: Length and area describe geometry; resistivity describes the material and condition.
Stretching a uniform wire changes both length and area under stated assumptions.
Metal resistivity usually rises with temperature over the introductory range.
chapters.script: Resistance has two layers. Geometry matters through R equals rho L over A, while resistivity rho belongs to the material and its physical condition. A longer uniform wire gives carriers more length over which collisions can impede drift. A larger cross section offers more parallel paths, so resistance falls. For a given metal over a modest temperature range, we often model resistivity as rho equals rho zero times one plus alpha times T minus T zero. Metals usually have positive alpha: heating increases resistivity. Semiconductors can behave differently, so do not transfer the metal sign automatically. Try a geometry question. A uniform wire is stretched to twice its original length, with volume conserved. If its radius becomes r prime, the volume relation says the new area is half the old area. Since resistance is proportional to L over A, the new resistance is two divided by one half, or four times the original. This answer uses a hidden assumption: uniform stretching and constant resistivity. If the wire is heated substantially, rho may change too, and the simple factor of four is incomplete. Another useful distinction: resistivity has units ohm meter and does not depend on the sample's length or area, while resistance has units ohm and does. A material can have low resistivity but still form a large resistance if made into a very long, thin wire. In a graph or numerical question, list what changed: material, temperature, length, area or all four. That checklist keeps geometry and material effects from getting mixed together.

chapters.title: Electrical power and energy
chapters.formula: P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R; electrical energy W = Pt
points: Power is the rate of electrical energy transfer.
Choose the form that matches the quantity held fixed.
A fixed-voltage comparison favors the lower resistance for higher power; a fixed-current comparison reverses that result.
chapters.script: Finally, let us track what the circuit is doing with energy. Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, P equals V I. For an ohmic resistor, substitute V equals I R to get P equals I squared R, or substitute I equals V over R to get P equals V squared over R. These forms are equivalent only when the same resistor model applies. The safest choice depends on what the question gives and what remains fixed. A six ohm heater carries two amperes. Its power is I squared R, which is four times six, or twenty four watts. In five minutes, the energy transferred is power times time: twenty four multiplied by three hundred seconds, or seven thousand two hundred joules. Now compare two resistors across the same ideal voltage. Since P equals V squared over R, the smaller resistance takes the larger power. With the same current through them, P equals I squared R, so the larger resistance takes the larger power. Same symbols, different constraint, different comparison. That is a classic JEE trap. Power is not the same as energy: watts measure joules per second, while energy is measured in joules. In a real resistor, electrical energy becomes internal energy and then often heat transferred to the surroundings. We have now built a clean foundation: charge flow gives current, the material and geometry give resistance, and voltage-current conditions determine power. The next classes will use these ideas in resistor networks, cells and Kirchhoff laws, where node-by-node bookkeeping becomes the main skill.

quiz.question: A section carries 12 C of charge in 4 s. Its average current is:
A wire carries 2 A through an area of 1 mm squared. Its current density is:
quiz.explanation: 1 mm squared is 1 x 10^-6 m squared, so J = 2/(1 x 10^-6) = 2 x 10^6 A/m squared.

quiz.question: A 12 V ohmic resistor carries 3 A. Its resistance is:
A uniform wire is stretched to twice its length while volume and resistivity stay constant. Its resistance becomes:
quiz.explanation: Area halves when volume is constant, so R is proportional to 2L divided by A/2, giving 4R.

quiz.question: A 6 ohm resistor carries 2 A. Its power is:
quiz.explanation: P = I squared R = 4 x 6 = 24 W.

quiz.question: Two resistors are connected across the same ideal voltage. Which has greater power in the ohmic model?
quiz.explanation: At fixed voltage, P = V squared/R, so the smaller resistance receives greater power.
